catalog_quote: Stress is heard on verb and noun stems, and tends to fall on the last member of a compound made up of more than one stem. Stressed syllables in the text below have longer vowels than unstressed syllables, and low-toned vowels are higher in pitch when stressed. High-toned vowels are not higher in pitch when stressed. Loanwords receive high or falling tone on the syllable stressed in the donor language. Stressed syllables may also be characterized by more distinct pronunciation of initial consonants: glottal stops are longer and more likely to have full closure in stem-initial position. [p. 109, 'Tones'] There are high, low and falling tones. Falling tones are often found in loanwords, apparently reflecting reinterpretation of stress in the donor language, but they also result from historical lenition and deletion of consonants.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Jicarilla is a tone language (high, low, falling); on top of tone, stress falls on the (verb or noun) stem syllable, i.e. the morphological root, which in Athabaskan word structure is word-final after the prefix string; in stem-stem compounds stress tends to go to the last stem. Stress is cued by vowel duration (and raised pitch on low-toned syllables, stronger stem-initial consonants), not by a positional count from a word edge. Hoijer 1943 (pan-Apachean, naming Jicarilla) instead describes evenly stressed syllables with syllable tonemes only; Tuttle 2000 (JASA abstract) confirms instrumentally that stressed syllables are distinguished by within-syllable duration despite final lengthening.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds of more than one stem: stress tends to fall on the last stem. Loanwords: high or falling tone placed on the syllable stressed in the donor language (stress reinterpreted as tone). High-toned vowels show no pitch raising under stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, based on one speaker (Merton Sandoval, Dulce NM) reading the North Wind text; the following 'Intonation in the text' section (pp. 110-111) reports strong utterance-final lengthening and little phrasal F0 manipulation, so stress claims are drawn from a read text rather than isolated citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Tuttle & Sandoval 2002 describe the speech of one speaker, Merton Sandoval of Dulce, New Mexico (Jicarilla Apache Nation), i.e. the standard jica1244 variety; no dialect split is invoked. Hoijer 1943 is a pan-Apachean generalization (examples Navaho) that names Jicarilla explicitly and claims evenly stressed syllables with syllable tonemes only, which is in tension with Tuttle & Sandoval's stem stress; the 2002 first-hand, single-language description is taken as the statement of record.
